new-nordic-cuisine.name: New Nordic Cuisine
new-nordic-cuisine.summary: A culinary movement developed in the Nordic countries since the mid-2000s, promoting local, natural and seasonal ingredients, launched by a 2004 Copenhagen manifesto.

arla-foods.name: Arla Foods
arla-foods.summary: A Danish/Swedish dairy co-operative formed in 2000 by merging Sweden's Arla with Denmark's MD Foods, now the world's fifth-largest dairy company.

kroppkaka.name: Kroppkakor
kroppkaka.summary: Traditional Swedish boiled potato dumpling, usually filled with onion and meat, eaten mainly in the southern Swedish provinces.

noma-restaurant.name: Noma
noma-restaurant.summary: A Copenhagen restaurant and food lab founded by René Redzepi and Claus Meyer in 2003, known for foraging and New Nordic cuisine and repeatedly named world's best restaurant.

international-whaling-commission.name: International Whaling Commission
international-whaling-commission.summary: An organization established in 1946 to regulate whaling worldwide and conserve whale stocks, setting catch limits, protected areas and species protections.

s-pmi.name: Sápmi
s-pmi.summary: The traditional homeland of the Sámi people, spanning northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, most of it north of the Arctic Circle.

nordic-council.name: Nordic Council
nordic-council.summary: The official body for inter-parliamentary cooperation among the Nordic countries, formed in 1952 with 87 representatives from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and related territories.

magnus-nilsson-chef.name: Magnus Nilsson
magnus-nilsson-chef.summary: Swedish chef who led the restaurant Fäviken until it closed in 2019, after earlier training in France; Fäviken won two Michelin stars and ranked among the world's best restaurants.

f-viken.name: Fäviken
f-viken.summary: A restaurant in rural Sweden run by chef Magnus Nilsson from 2008 to 2019, named among the World's 50 Best Restaurants in 2012 and one of the world's top ten by Zagat in 2013.

arctic-cathedral.name: Arctic Cathedral
arctic-cathedral.summary: Nickname for Tromsdalen Church, a 1965 concrete and metal parish church in Tromsø, Norway, whose shape is thought to echo a nearby twin-peaked island.

jan-inge-hovig.name: Jan Inge Hovig
jan-inge-hovig.summary: Norwegian architect (1920–1977) who worked on Narvik's postwar reconstruction before designing the Arctic Cathedral, finished in 1965 and probably Tromsø's most famous building.

h-ja.name: Håja
h-ja.summary: Uninhabited island near Hammerfest in northern Norway, known for a gull colony and traditional egg- and berry-picking, and the namesake of local institutions.

bauhaus.name: Bauhaus
bauhaus.summary: A German art and design school founded by Walter Gropius in 1919, combining crafts and fine arts and later closed in 1933 under Nazi pressure, hugely influential in modern design and architecture.

arne-jacobsen.name: Arne Jacobsen
arne-jacobsen.summary: Danish architect and furniture designer (1902–1971) known for architectural functionalism and worldwide success with simple, well-designed chairs.

egg-chair.name: Egg chair
egg-chair.summary: Chair designed by Arne Jacobsen in 1959 for the SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen, and an icon of Danish design.

poul-henningsen.name: Poul Henningsen
poul-henningsen.summary: A Danish author, critic, architect and designer (1894–1967), a leading cultural figure between the World Wars, best known for his glare-free, shaded PH-lamp series.

ph-lamp.name: PH-lamp
ph-lamp.summary: A light fixture designed by Danish designer Poul Henningsen, using concentric shades to hide the bulb and eliminate glare; first shown in 1925.

harry-haerendel.name: Harry Haerendel
harry-haerendel.summary: German artist from Hamburg (1893–1982), best known for his painting Der alte Seebär, depicting a bearded old sailor smoking a pipe, later popular in Scandinavia as kitsch art.

brooklyn-museum.name: Brooklyn Museum
brooklyn-museum.summary: Art museum in Brooklyn, New York City's second largest, holding around 500,000 objects including a major collection of Egyptian antiquities.

functionalism-architecture.name: Functionalism (architecture)
functionalism-architecture.summary: A principle that buildings should be designed based solely on their purpose, forming an international movement after World War I linked to socialism and modern humanism, strongest in Czechoslovakia, Germany, Poland, the USSR and the Netherlands.

victor-sparre.name: Victor Sparre
victor-sparre.summary: Norwegian painter, glass designer and non-fiction writer (1919–2008).

lunning-prize.name: Lunning Prize
lunning-prize.summary: An award given to two leading Scandinavian designers each year from 1951 to 1970, instrumental in defining and promoting Scandinavian Design.

jugendstil.name: Jugendstil
jugendstil.summary: An artistic movement in the decorative arts influential in Germany and Austria from about 1895 to 1910, the German-Austrian counterpart to Art Nouveau, reacting against academic historicism.

edvard-munch.name: Edvard Munch
edvard-munch.summary: A Norwegian painter (1863-1944) whose 1893 work The Scream became one of the most iconic images in Western art, emerging from a childhood shadowed by illness and bereavement.

vilhelm-hammersh-i.name: Vilhelm Hammershøi
vilhelm-hammersh-i.summary: Danish painter (1864–1916) known for subdued, poetic portraits and interior scenes, praised by poet Rainer Maria Rilke as an artist whose work speaks to what is essential in art.

iceland-university-of-the-arts.name: Iceland Academy of the Arts
iceland-university-of-the-arts.summary: An Icelandic institution of higher art education in Reykjavík, founded in 1998 by merging the Iceland Drama School and the Reykjavík Arts School, offering the country's only university-level arts degrees.

wehrmacht.name: Wehrmacht
wehrmacht.summary: The unified armed forces of Nazi Germany from 1935 to 1945, combining the army, navy and air force, central to Germany's power in World War II.

winter-war.name: Winter War
winter-war.summary: War between the Soviet Union and Finland from November 1939 to March 1940, in which Finland resisted despite Soviet superiority before the Moscow Peace Treaty.

harry-martinson.name: Harry Martinson
harry-martinson.summary: Swedish writer, poet and former sailor (1904–1978) who shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Literature with fellow Swede Eyvind Johnson, a controversial choice since both were Swedish Academy members.

aniara.name: Aniara
aniara.summary: A 1956 Swedish epic science-fiction poem by Nobel laureate Harry Martinson, about a spacecraft of refugees drifting off course after leaving a doomed Earth; translated into about twenty languages and adapted into an opera and film.

eyvind-johnson.name: Eyvind Johnson
eyvind-johnson.summary: Swedish novelist (1900–1976) considered the most groundbreaking figure in modern Swedish literature, who shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Literature with Harry Martinson.

sigrid-undset.name: Sigrid Undset
sigrid-undset.summary: A Danish-born Norwegian novelist (1882–1949) awarded the 1928 Nobel Prize in Literature, best known for her medieval trilogy Kristin Lavransdatter.

halld-r-laxness.name: Halldór Laxness
halld-r-laxness.summary: Icelandic writer (1902-1998) who won the 1955 Nobel Prize in Literature for his novels, poetry and other works.

tomas-transtr-mer.name: Tomas Tranströmer
tomas-transtr-mer.summary: Swedish poet, psychologist and translator (1931–2015) known for poems about nature and mystery, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Literature.

krilon.name: Krilon
krilon.summary: Trilogy of novels (1941–1943) by Eyvind Johnson, part realistic Stockholm story and part allegory criticising Nazism, fascism and Sweden's wartime neutrality.

bruno-k-ijer.name: Bruno K. Öijer
bruno-k-ijer.summary: Contemporary Swedish poet, born 26 November 1951 in Linköping.

antonin-artaud.name: Antonin Artaud
antonin-artaud.summary: French artist and writer (1896–1948) recognized as a major figure of the European avant-garde, whose concept of the Theatre of Cruelty strongly influenced 20th-century theatre.

theatre-of-cruelty.name: Theatre of Cruelty
theatre-of-cruelty.summary: A form of theatre devised by Antonin Artaud that breaks from traditional Western theatre to assault the senses of the audience, influencing artists like Jerzy Grotowski and Peter Brook.

yvind-fahlstr-m.name: Öyvind Fahlström
yvind-fahlstr-m.summary: A Brazilian-born Swedish multimedia artist, 1928 to 1976.

ke-hodell.name: Åke Hodell
ke-hodell.summary: Swedish fighter pilot, poet, author, text-sound composer and artist (1919-2000).

quisling-regime.name: Quisling regime
quisling-regime.summary: The collaborationist puppet government led by Vidkun Quisling in German-occupied Norway during the Second World War, though real power stayed with the German Reichskommissar.

maastricht-treaty.name: Maastricht Treaty
maastricht-treaty.summary: 1992 foundation treaty of the European Union that introduced shared citizenship, plans for a single currency, and closer foreign and security cooperation.

h-vam-l.name: Hávamál
h-vam-l.summary: Old Norse poem attributed to Odin, dated to around 900–1000 CE, offering practical and philosophical wisdom on conduct, plus an account of how Odin won the runes.

odin.name: Odin
odin.summary: A widely revered god of Norse mythology and Germanic paganism, associated with wisdom, poetry and frenzy, worshipped from Roman-era Germania through the Viking Age.

axel-h-gerstr-m.name: Axel Hägerström
axel-h-gerstr-m.summary: Swedish philosopher (1868 to 1939) who founded the Uppsala school of philosophy and the Scandinavian legal realism movement. He opposed the then dominant idealism in Swedish philosophy.

uppsala-university.name: Uppsala University
uppsala-university.summary: Public research university in Uppsala, Sweden, founded in 1477 as the oldest in Sweden and the Nordic countries. It gained stability from a large donation by King Gustavus Adolphus in the early 1600s.

christopher-jacob-bostr-m.name: Christopher Jacob Boström
christopher-jacob-bostr-m.summary: Swedish philosopher (1797 to 1866) whose ideas dominated Swedish philosophy until the early twentieth century. He also strongly influenced Swedish cultural life.

arne-n-ss.name: Arne Næss
arne-n-ss.summary: Norwegian philosopher (1912 to 2009) who coined the term "deep ecology". He drew on Rachel Carson's Silent Spring and argued that environmental problems come from unspoken Western philosophical attitudes.

deep-ecology.name: Deep ecology
deep-ecology.summary: Environmental philosophy holding that all living beings have inherent worth regardless of their usefulness to humans, and that modern human societies should be restructured in line with this idea.

knud-ejler-l-gstrup.name: Knud Ejler Løgstrup
knud-ejler-l-gstrup.summary: Danish philosopher and Lutheran theologian (1905–1981). Thinkers such as Alasdair MacIntyre, Simon Critchley and Zygmunt Bauman have discussed his work.

lee-m-hollander.name: Lee M. Hollander
lee-m-hollander.summary: An American philologist (1880–1972) who specialized in Old Norse studies and led the Germanic Languages department at the University of Texas at Austin.

s-ren-kierkegaard.name: Søren Kierkegaard
s-ren-kierkegaard.summary: A Danish philosopher, theologian, poet and social critic (1813–1855) widely considered the first existentialist, known for stressing authenticity and personal choice in how one lives as an individual.

howard-mumford-jones.name: Howard Mumford Jones
howard-mumford-jones.summary: American intellectual historian, literary critic, journalist and poet (1892–1980) who taught English at the University of Michigan and Harvard University.

karl-olivecrona.name: Karl Olivecrona
karl-olivecrona.summary: Swedish lawyer and legal philosopher (1897–1980), professor at Lund University. He stressed the psychological side of legal ideas and argued that a monopoly of force is the basis of law.

alf-ross.name: Alf Ross
alf-ross.summary: Danish jurist and legal philosopher (1899–1979), a leading figure of Scandinavian legal realism. He also served as a judge of the European Court of Human Rights from 1959 to 1971.

anders-vilhelm-lundstedt.name: Anders Vilhelm Lundstedt
anders-vilhelm-lundstedt.summary: Swedish jurist and legislator (1882–1955), a proponent of Scandinavian Legal Realism and professor of law at Uppsala from 1914 to 1947. He argued that no objective way exists to define justice, and he sat in the Swedish parliament for many years.

georg-henrik-von-wright.name: Georg Henrik von Wright
georg-henrik-von-wright.summary: Finnish philosopher (1916-2003) known for his work in philosophical logic, especially deontic logic, and on Ludwig Wittgenstein's later philosophy.

deontic-logic.name: Deontic logic
deontic-logic.summary: Field of philosophical logic concerned with obligation, permission and related concepts. It is also a formal system that tries to capture the essential logical features of those ideas.

ludwig-wittgenstein.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
ludwig-wittgenstein.summary: Austro-British philosopher (1889–1951) working in logic and philosophy of language, born into a wealthy Viennese family and educated under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge.

h-l-a-hart.name: H. L. A. Hart
h-l-a-hart.summary: British legal philosopher (1907-1992) and one of the most influential legal theorists of the 20th century. He helped develop legal positivism in his book The Concept of Law and was Oxford's Professor of Jurisprudence from 1952 to 1969.

legal-realism.name: Legal realism
legal-realism.summary: Approach to law holding that it should be studied with the empirical methods of natural science, focusing on law as it is actually practiced rather than as it ought to be.

tidehverv.name: Tidehverv
tidehverv.summary: Danish theological movement and periodical, called the most influential in Denmark. It began as a Grundtvigian reaction against liberal theology and turned national conservative in the late 20th century.

experimental-philosophy.name: Experimental philosophy
experimental-philosophy.summary: Field of philosophy, called x-phi for short, that uses empirical data, often surveys of ordinary people's intuitions, to inform philosophical questions. It contrasts with "armchair" philosophy based mainly on a priori reasoning.

church-of-sweden.name: Church of Sweden
church-of-sweden.summary: Sweden's largest Christian denomination and former state church, a high-church Lutheran body headquartered in Uppsala and led by its archbishop.

viking-revival.name: Viking revival
viking-revival.summary: A late-18th- and 19th-century movement of renewed, often romanticized interest in Viking history and culture, part of the broader Romantic era.

zuism.name: Zuism
zuism.summary: A modern Neopagan movement based on ancient Sumerian-Mesopotamian and Semitic-Canaanite religions, whose Icelandic branch gained state recognition from 2013 as a protest against the church tax.

ama-gi.name: Amargi
ama-gi.summary: A Sumerian word for release from debt, slavery, taxation or punishment, regarded as the earliest known written reference to the idea of freedom.
